rationale: Start with a broad mid-temperature scouting gradient to elute all 8 compounds if possible and map the overall elution window without being excessively steep or long. This should reveal whether the sample spans most of the organic range and whether any compounds risk truncation or early unretained elution.

All compounds eluted between about 4 and 9.4 min in the first run, corresponding roughly to a narrow effective elution window near phi 0.20–0.44, so trimming the gradient to that region should make it much shallower where the peaks actually separate. Keeping tG and T fixed isolates the effect of narrowing the phi window on the critical 4/5 pair.

Narrowing the phi window changed selectivity badly, so the critical overlap is likely not solved by window trimming alone. A pure slope test against injection 1 will show whether the bad pair is slope-responsive; if resolution improves substantially, we can later shorten from there, and if not, we should pivot to temperature.

The critical pair is strongly slope-responsive: doubling tG fully resolved all pairs, so now the right move is to shorten from 40 min toward the minimum tG that still keeps every pair at R at least 1.5 while staying under the 10 min last-peak threshold. A moderate step to 24 min should test whether full resolution can be retained near the time optimum.

At 40 C the pair near rows 4/5 remains under-resolved at practical tG, while it is slope-responsive, so a temperature increase may shift selectivity enough to resolve it without needing the full 40 min gradient. Using 22 min keeps us near the likely time optimum if T improves that critical pair.

Raising temperature hurt selectivity badly, so the next clean orthogonal test is lowering T while holding phi-window and tG fixed to see whether the critical close pair opens instead. This directly probes whether cooler conditions improve selectivity enough to keep a near-optimal runtime.

Temperature shifts just moved the coelution elsewhere, so 40 C still looks best and the key leverage remains gradient slope. Since 24 min was insufficient and 40 min over-resolved with a time penalty, test 28 min at 40 C to bracket the minimum tG that may fully resolve all pairs.

Resolution improves strongly with longer tG at 40 C, and 28 min is still not enough while 40 min is more than needed, so 32 min is the next efficient bracket toward the shortest fully resolved method. This should clarify whether complete resolution is achievable near the practical optimum or if 36 min will be required.

The changing worst pair with tG suggests at least one elution-order crossover or strong selectivity evolution along the gradient, so we should complete the slope map at 40 C with 36 min rather than keep guessing. This will show whether the full-resolution region is narrow and near 40 min or whether we need to change the phi window instead.

Since broad-window slope changes at 40 C do not give a practical win and temperature changes shift which pair is critical, try an intermediate temperature at the best time-efficient tG of 20 min. This may nudge selectivity enough to resolve the 4/5 overlap without introducing the severe new coelutions seen at 30 or 50 C.

45 C at 20 min is now the best point and only two pairs remain slightly below full credit, so the most likely gain is a small reduction in gradient steepness while keeping the favorable selectivity. Moving to 22 min should improve both critical pairs with only a small risk of crossing the 10 min last-peak limit.

At 20 min, 45 C improved selectivity markedly over 40 C, but 50 C became worse, so the optimum may be temperature-specific rather than slope-driven. Testing 35 C at the same fast gradient probes the other side of 40 C to see whether one of the two near-critical pairs can be pushed above 1.5 without sacrificing runtime.

The temperature trend is nonmonotonic and 45 C is best so far, but we have not yet mapped the high-temperature end at the same optimal 20 min slope. A 60 C run could produce another selectivity crossover that separates both marginal pairs while keeping the chromatogram comfortably under 10 min.

60 C at 20 min is the current best and leaves only one pair slightly under 1.5, so the most promising refinement is a small decrease in slope while keeping the favorable high-temperature selectivity. A 22 min gradient should improve the remaining 5/6 pair and still likely keep the last peak under 10 min.

At 60 C the remaining critical pair worsened when tG increased from 20 to 22 min, implying this pair benefits from a steeper gradient at that temperature. Testing 18 min should show whether we can push that last pair to full resolution while keeping the run even shorter.

Injection 15 is nearly ideal: all pairs are at full credit except one just below threshold, and the run is already very fast. Testing 16 min checks whether the critical pair can cross or stay near 1.5 with an even shorter method, which could reach the maximum CRF if selectivity continues to favor the steeper gradient.

The optimum appears very sharp around 18 min and 60 C, with 16 min too steep and 20 min shifting the critical pair. A small temperature decrease at the best tG may nudge the remaining 3/4 pair above 1.5 without sacrificing the excellent runtime.

The best condition is extremely close to full credit, so the remaining leverage is likely from a slight change in the phi window rather than more slope or temperature changes. Narrowing the broad window modestly while keeping the center similar should alter gradient selectivity enough to test whether the last 3/4 pair can be pushed over R = 1.5.

The narrowed window at 18 min is essentially optimal, with only one pair at R 1.49, so the safest path to full credit is a minimal reduction in slope while preserving the improved selectivity from the 0.10–0.90 window. A 20 min run should test whether that last pair crosses 1.5 while still keeping t_last comfortably below 10 min.

Since 0.10–0.90 at 18 min was essentially perfect and making the gradient shallower hurt the same late pair, the better next move is a small upward shift of the window to alter local selectivity around the mid-late peaks while keeping the favorable steepness. Raising phi0 to 0.15 may move the tightly spaced 5/6 pair just enough to cross full-resolution credit.

The 0.10–0.90 window at 18 min is closest to perfect, and shifting phi0 upward disturbed the early critical cluster, so keep phi0 at 0.10 and instead lower phi1 one step. This narrows the window and slightly changes the local slope/selectivity for the later 5/6 pair that was just short of full credit.

Lowering phi1 hurt the late critical pair, so try the opposite direction from the near-optimal 0.10–0.90 method. Raising phi1 to 0.95 while keeping phi0 and tG fixed may slightly steepen the late part of the gradient and nudge the 5/6 pair over the 1.5 threshold without disrupting the already good early separations.

The best window found is 0.10–0.90, and around that window the optimum may sit between the tested slopes of 16 min (broad window) and 18 min. Testing 16 min with the improved 0.10–0.90 window checks whether the steeper slope can convert the near-miss 5/6 pair into full resolution while preserving the other adjacent pairs.

The best result came from 0.10–0.90 at 18 min, with only one late pair at R 1.49, while shifting phi1 worsened that pair and raising phi0 hurt the early cluster. Lowering phi0 one step while keeping phi1 and tG fixed is the remaining logical local perturbation to test whether the late pair gains the tiny extra selectivity needed without breaking the already adequate early separations.

The best method, 0.10–0.90 at 18 min and 60 C, missed a perfect score by only 0.01 on one late pair, so the last worthwhile test is a small temperature decrease at that exact window and slope to probe a final selectivity nudge. It is the only local degree of freedom around the best point not yet tested.
